intro: Invariant finds data center sites for buyers across the US, from energized 1 MW edge and mining sites to a 1.5 GW AI campus. The method is the same at every size: start from power evidence, rule out sites that cannot close, then match land. This page sets out what each size needs, how to grade a site’s power, the 2026 rules that change the search, and the sites we have now. Tell us your MW, states and date, and we send the ones that fit.
takeaways: Search from power first. Land is rarely the constraint; deliverable MW on a date is.
Grade each site by the document behind its MW: map, proximity, named MW, utility study, signed agreement.
Size changes everything: 1 to 10 MW sits on distribution, 20 to 100 MW needs a substation, 200 MW and up is a transmission project.

sections.heading: Start from power, not land

blocks.text: Most data center site searches start with a parcel and a line on a map. That is backwards. Land is plentiful almost everywhere in the US. Deliverable power on a known date is not. In a 2025 analysis of ERCOT, Paces found only about 17% of substations near suitable land had any withdrawal headroom. The rest of the land was stranded.

So the search runs in this order. Pick the MW and the date. Find stations, plants and energized loads that can carry it. Kill anything claimed, contaminated or under a moratorium. Then look at parcels around what survives. Finally, grade each site by the document behind its MW.

description: Find a 1 MW data center site in the US: energized edge, inference and mining sites, what 1 MW really fits, the service you need and how fast it can be live.
intro: A 1 MW data center site is the easiest size to find and the easiest to get wrong. At this scale you are almost always on the utility distribution system, so the fastest sites are buildings or yards that already have the service in place. A new 1 MW service can take longer than people expect because of transformer lead times and feeder upgrades. Invariant keeps a running list of energized small sites across the US, from 0.5 MW turnkey mining yards to Tier III rooms, and shares the ones that fit on a call.
takeaways: 1 MW at the meter is about 0.75 MW of IT at a PUE of 1.3. That is roughly six 120 kW AI racks, or a few hundred air-cooled mining machines.
At this size the question is the existing service: voltage, transformer rating and whether the feeder has room. A site that already has it can be live in weeks.
Land is rarely the issue. A containerized 1 MW deployment fits on well under an acre.
Ask for a recent utility bill or a service letter showing the transformer and the contracted capacity, not a map of nearby lines.

blocks.text: Utilities sell facility load. Tenants buy IT load. At a PUE of 1.3, a 1 MW site leaves about 0.8 MW for IT. sections.heading: Where 1 MW sites come from

blocks.text: Most 1 MW sites we see are one of four things: a light industrial building with a large existing service, a small mining yard with containers already wired, a room inside a colocation facility, or a spot inside the fence of a power plant or industrial user that has spare capacity on its own transformers.

Each has a different catch. Industrial buildings often have the amps but not the cooling. Mining yards have power and airflow but no redundancy. Colocation rooms are fast and expensive per kW. Plant sites can be the cheapest power you will ever see, with the least flexibility on hours and terms.

blocks.text: Confirm the contracted capacity on the bill, not the panel rating. A building with a 4,000 A switchboard at 480 V can in theory carry more than 3 MW, yet its utility contract and transformer may cap it far lower.
Ask whether the power is firm or interruptible. Many small mining sites run on curtailable rates. That suits miners and does not suit an inference customer with an uptime promise.
